lead: Hypermedia is a set of media nodes — pages, images, audio, video — joined by links. A link lets a reader jump from one node to another, or start a clip at a fixed moment. Hypermedia messaging carries those links between systems so that every copy of a site agrees on what points where, and when linked media should play. It is used in web sites, e-learning modules, museum guides and streaming catalogues.
prereq: You need: 6.1 and Unit 5 on authoring and presentation structure.

blocks.text: A node is one addressable media object: an HTML page, a JPEG image, a 30-second audio clip, a video segment. An anchor is a marked place inside a node — a word, a paragraph, a rectangle in an image, a time range in a clip. A link is a directed connection from a source anchor to a target node or target anchor. Write it as a pair (s, t): s is the source anchor, t is the target.

Hypertext has text nodes only. Hypermedia allows images, audio, video and animation as nodes. The prefix hyper means beyond linear reading: the reader chooses the next node. A 1990s CD-ROM encyclopedia was hypermedia; a web page with an embedded video is hypermedia today.

A static link is stored with the document. In HTML, code such as href="unit6.html" is a static link: the address is in the file. A search engine builds result links from your query; a recommendation engine links “customers also watched”. A dynamic link is not stored in the document file. A program builds it at request time from a database, query or user profile and writes it into the page before sending it; so the stored file has no fixed address for it.

blocks.text: In time-based hypermedia a link fixes when the target plays, not only where it appears. Clicking a word in a lecture transcript may start the video at 00:12 and stop it at 00:20. The link carries a time interval [t₁, t₂]. t₁ is the start time in seconds; t₂ is the end time in seconds. This is common in e-learning and sports replays. Presentation-level synchronisation belongs to Unit 4; here the focus is the link record.

The Dexter model is a reference model for hypertext systems. It splits a system into the storage layer (nodes, links and anchors as stored), the within-component layer (the inside of one node, where anchors are marked) and the run-time layer (what is presented now). The model exists so that one link database can serve different presentations.

Link integrity means every link has a live source and target. A dangling link points to a node or anchor that no longer exists. It causes a dead jump or a 404. Systems check links after every content change.

Hypermedia messaging is the set of messages that create, update or delete links. A create message carries source id, target id, link type and timing. An update message changes the target or the time interval. A delete message removes the link and may leave a tombstone. A content management system sends these messages to caches and delivery nodes so all copies agree.
A path is a sequence of nodes joined by links. Its length is the number of links, not the number of nodes. Three nodes in a row give two clicks: Home, FAQ, Notes. This is the trap examiners use.

blocks.where: |P| is the number of clicks along path P; n is the number of nodes visited.

examples.question: A hypermedia site has these links: Home → Courses, Courses → Unit6, Unit6 → Notes, Home → Contact, Contact → FAQ, FAQ → Notes, Home → FAQ. Find the fewest clicks from Home to Notes and list the path.
steps: Write the adjacency list: Home → {Courses, Contact, FAQ}; Courses → {Unit6}; Unit6 → {Notes}; Contact → {FAQ}; FAQ → {Notes}; Notes → {}.
Start at Home with 0 clicks. Its direct neighbours are Courses, Contact and FAQ, so each is at 1 click. Notes is not among them.
From FAQ at 1 click, the link FAQ → Notes reaches Notes at 2 clicks. The path is Home → FAQ → Notes.
The longer paths are Home → Contact → FAQ → Notes and Home → Courses → Unit6 → Notes. Each uses 3 links, so both are longer.
Home → FAQ → Notes visits 3 nodes and uses 2 links. The answer is the link count, 2 clicks.
examples.answer: The fewest clicks from Home to Notes is 2 clicks, by the path Home → FAQ → Notes; the Courses path uses 3 links.

traps: Counting nodes instead of links: Home → FAQ → Notes has three nodes but two clicks.
Calling every link hypermedia: hypertext has text nodes only; hypermedia adds images, audio and video.
Treating dynamic links as stored: the address is created per request by a program, so the saved document file does not contain it.
Forgetting that a link can carry time: a time-based link also sets when the target starts and stops.

Confusing a dangling link with a broken node: a link is dangling when its target node or its target anchor is gone. Both break link integrity; a missing node needs the link deleted or retargeted, a missing anchor on a live node can also be repaired by re-marking the anchor.

quiz.q: Define node, anchor and link in one sentence each.
quiz.a: A node is an addressable media object. An anchor is a marked place inside a node. A link is a directed connection from a source anchor to a target node or anchor.

quiz.q: Why is a dynamic link not stored in the document file?
quiz.a: The address is not fixed in the stored file; a program generates it at request time from a database, query or user profile and inserts it into the page that is sent.

quiz.q: Using the figure, how many clicks from Home to Contact?
quiz.a: 1 click: Home → Contact is one direct link.

quiz.q: A link points to a video that was deleted. Name the fault and the message that repairs it.
quiz.a: The fault is a dangling link. A delete or update link message removes or retargets the link so link integrity is restored.

quiz.q: State two differences between hypertext and hypermedia.
quiz.a: Hypertext has text nodes only; hypermedia allows images, audio and video. Hypermedia may also carry timing on links; plain hypertext usually does not.

quiz.q: What does a time-based link store beyond source and target?
quiz.a: It stores a time interval [t₁, t₂]: t₁ is when the target starts playing and t₂ is when it stops, in seconds.

quiz.q: A path visits four nodes. How many clicks does it use? Explain with an example.
quiz.a: 3 clicks. A path A → B → C → D visits four nodes and has three links, so it needs three clicks.

quiz.q: Given the path Home → FAQ → Notes, how many clicks and how many nodes?
quiz.a: 2 clicks and 3 nodes. The click count is the number of links, which is one less than the number of nodes.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern web APIs use hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS): a response carries links that tell the client what it may do next. Adaptive hypermedia changes links to fit each learner's progress. Research systems combine time-based links with MPEG-7 metadata so a search can jump to a scene, not just a file. Search for “Dexter model”, “adaptive hypermedia” and “link integrity checking”.
